chunks: "Via stitching means placing a lot of vias that tie copper of the same net together between layers, typically ground, so the layers behave as one low-impedance conductor.
You see rows of them around the edge of a board, along an RF trace, or in a grid across a pour. There are a few reasons to do it.
First, return paths: if a fast signal hops from one layer to another, its return current has to hop between ground planes too, so you put a ground via right next to the signal via.

Second, shielding: a fence of vias along both sides of an RF trace, or around the board edge, acts like a wall, and the rule of thumb is to space them closer than a twentieth of a wavelength at the highest frequency you care about, which gives about 20 decibels of shielding from the gap leakage.
Third, current and heat: a pour that has to carry amps between layers needs an array of vias, and thermal vias under a hot IC carry heat to other layers.
Fourth, you stop big plane pairs resonating and avoid floating copper islands. I don't just add them everywhere, though.
Too many in a row can chop up the plane, and they cost drill time."
